title: Японцы отказались от рыбы  (The Japanese Refuse the Fish)

segments.t: Waiters carry all the fish dishes back to the kitchen because the Japanese delegation immediately smelled that the fish wasn't fresh. Mikhail Jekovich deducts the cost from the cooks' wages, and Senya stubbornly eats a piece to prove them wrong.
Потому что она совсем не свежая.
Стоимость блюд я вычту у вас.
Не надо моих гостей кормить этим.
Now let's go back through their conversation line by line and unpack the Russian phrasing.
'The waiters are carrying your fish back.' Fedya picks one colorful choice right here: "ofitsianty" means "waiters" (from "ofitsiant"), giving the line its exact edge.
'The Japanese refused to eat this fish.' Mikhail follows up openly with a sigh, so Senya knows he is not just making small talk.
Потому что она совсем не свежая.
'Because it is not fresh at all.' Mikhail responds firmly during the talk, before Fedya can change the subject.
Стоимость блюд я вычту у вас.
'I will deduct the cost of the dishes from you.' Mikhail uses one pointed detail in earnest: "stoimost" means "to cost", and it carries the main weight of what Mikhail is saying.
'Wow, that is quite a fine.' Fedya puts that point for Mikhail: notice how Russian needs no word for "am", "is", or "are" in the present — placing the words side by side says it all.
Не надо моих гостей кормить этим.
'Do not feed my guests with this.' Mikhail cuts in pointedly around Senya, shifting the whole mood of the room in a single beat.
'By the way, this is very tasty fish.' Senya anchors one colorful detail for Fedya: "vkusnaya" means "tasty" (from "vkusnyy"), giving the line its exact edge.

'The Japanese simply do not understand anything.' Senya voices this warning plainly here: the little word "prosto" ("simply, just") works like a shrug in the sentence, making a big claim sound effortless.
'Well, how do you like our fish?' Fedya tests briskly about what Mikhail just brought up.
'The discounted fish went down well!' Senya spotlights this key piece on cue: "skidkoy" means "discount" (from "skidka"), giving the line its exact edge.
'Senya, what is wrong with you right now?' Fedya shares that answer calmly now: notice how Russian needs no word for "am", "is", or "are" in the present — placing the words side by side says it all.
'I need to step out urgently for a minute.' Senya jumps in promptly watching Mikhail, making his position completely clear.
Потому что она совсем не свежая.
Стоимость блюд я вычту у вас.
Не надо моих гостей кормить этим.
Senya's stomach immediately rebels against the bargain fish, while Mikhail sneaks his pony inside the hotel for the night. Until next time!
